location: Pacific Ocean, 2.7 miles north of Anacapa Island, California
the_unresolved_thing: The lubrication interval on the jackscrew was extended four times between 1987 and 1996 and the FAA approved every extension. No investigation established what data the FAA believed it was reviewing.

structural_test.why: Approval chain, not failure sequence. Four approvals, no supporting data on the record.

commonly_wrong.record: The jackscrew survived. The acme nut riding on it lost its threads; roughly 90% had already worn away.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: Confusing the shaft with the nut misattributes the failure mode entirely.

commonly_wrong.record: The interval itself was extended, repeatedly and with approval. The NTSB named the extensions and the FAA's approval of them as contributing causes.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: It was not an individual lapse. It was an authorised schedule.

commonly_wrong.record: In 1997 a lead mechanic found the end play at its 0.040 inch limit and ordered the assembly replaced. The aircraft returned to service days later with it installed.
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: There is a documented flag on this exact assembly, years early.

slides.text: Everyone aboard Alaska Airlines Flight 261 died in the Pacific, 2.7 miles north of Anacapa Island, on 31 January 2000.

slides.label: What everyone gets wrong
slides.headline: The jackscrew never broke.
slides.text: The shaft survived the impact. What failed was the acme nut riding on it. Roughly 90% of its threads had already worn away before the aircraft ever left the gate.

slides.label: The barrier
slides.headline: One screw. No backup.
slides.text: The MD-80 horizontal stabilizer is driven by a single jackscrew. Lose the acme nut threads and you lose pitch control entirely. There is no second system.

slides.label: The document
slides.headline: 0.040 inches. Replace it.
slides.text: In 1997 a lead mechanic measured the end play at its maximum allowable limit and ordered the assembly replaced. The aircraft was back in service within days, same part fitted.

slides.label: The interval
slides.headline: 500 hours became 2,550.
slides.text: The lubrication interval was extended four times between 1987 and 1996. By July 1996 it stood at eight calendar months. The end play inspection interval was stretched as well.

slides.label: Who approved it
slides.headline: The FAA signed all four.
slides.text: Every extension was authorised. The NTSB found no supporting data was offered for any of them, and named both the extensions and their approval as contributing causes.
83 passengers and 5 crew. There were no survivors.

slides.label: Unresolved
slides.headline: Reviewing what, exactly?
slides.text: No investigation ever established what data the FAA believed it was assessing when it approved four consecutive extensions to the interval that kept this assembly alive.

source_line: NTSB Aircraft Accident Report NTSB/AAR-02/01, 10 December 2002; NTSB Docket DCA00MA023.
caption:
The jackscrew on Alaska 261 never broke. The nut riding on it lost its threads.

The lubrication interval for that assembly started at 500 flight hours. By 1996 it had been extended four times, to roughly 2,550. The FAA approved every extension and the NTSB found no supporting data was offered for any of them.

Source: NTSB Aircraft Accident Report AAR-02/01; NTSB Docket DCA00MA023.

slides.headline: 44 minutes. 2,000 rounds. Nobody died.
slides.text: Eleven officers and seven bystanders were hit outside a Bank of America in North Hollywood on 28 February 1997. Every one of them lived.

slides.label: What everyone gets wrong
slides.headline: They weren't armor-piercing rounds.
slides.text: The press said armor-piercing. The record says standard 7.62x39 and 5.56 rifle ammunition. What beat the officers was the gap between a handgun and a rifle, not exotic bullets.

slides.label: The barrier
slides.headline: A 9mm against a rifle plate.
slides.text: Patrol officers carried 9mm sidearms, .38 revolvers and shotguns. The robbers wore homemade Type III-A armor with a trauma plate. Nothing the officers carried went through it.

slides.label: The document
slides.headline: Buckshot only.
slides.text: LAPD patrol shotguns were restricted to buckshot. That single ammunition choice is the reason the one long gun on scene could not answer the threat.

slides.label: The signal
slides.headline: 9:33 a.m.
slides.text: Sixteen minutes into the firefight, officers confirmed what they were shooting at was armored. Until that moment they were still firing rounds that could not work.

slides.label: The improvisation
slides.headline: They borrowed the rifles.
slides.text: Officers drove to a gun shop three blocks away and commandeered AR-15s off the rack. A department of nine thousand officers armed itself mid-incident from a retail shelf.

slides.label: The clock
slides.headline:
09:17 first shots
09:33 armor confirmed
09:35 rifles commandeered
10:01 last shot fired
18 wounded. 0 killed.
slides.text: Both robbers died. Every officer and bystander who was hit survived, several because rounds passed through unarmored gaps rather than through anything the department had issued.

slides.label: Unresolved
slides.headline: Nobody signed it.
slides.text: The 1998 Use of Force Review Board report never establishes who restricted patrol shotguns to buckshot, on what ballistic grounds, or whether that decision was ever formally reviewed.

44 minutes. Over 2,000 rounds fired. 11 officers and 7 bystanders wounded. Zero deaths among them.

Two robbers in homemade body armor fought LAPD patrol officers carrying handguns and buckshot-loaded shotguns. None of it penetrated. Officers eventually got rifles by commandeering them from a gun store three blocks away.

The 1998 Use of Force Review Board report never establishes who restricted patrol shotguns to buckshot in the first place.

case_name: Apollo 13 Service Module Oxygen Tank 2 Explosion
location: Space, 205,000 miles from Earth en route to Moon
coordinates: N/A (deep space, approx. 205,000 miles from Earth)
the_number: Oxygen Tank 2, serial number 10024X-TA0009, exploded at 55 hours 55 minutes into flight
the_unresolved_thing: Who was accountable for enforcing the thermostat voltage change across the contractor chain, what documentation was supposed to flow the requirement down from ASPO through North American Rockwell to Beech Aircraft, and why no testing procedure ever required the switches to cycle under load at 65V before the tanks were qualified for flight.

structural_test.why: The Cortright Commission identified a definite approval chain failure: NASA's Apollo Spacecraft Program Office (ASPO) directed that Kennedy Space Center ground support equipment (GSE) supply 65V DC to oxygen tank heaters. North American Rockwell (NR), the prime contractor, was responsible for flowing this change down to subcontractors such as Beech Aircraft Corporation. North American Aviation and ASPO ordered Beech to fit a 65-volt thermostat switch in all Block 2 tanks, but Beech did not do it and the program office did not follow up. The discrepancy was not detected by NASA, NR, or Beech in their review of documentation, nor did tests identify the incompatibility, since neither qualification nor acceptance testing required switch cycling under load. This is not a failure-sequence timing dispute; it is an unresolved authorization gap: no investigation established what data the three parties believed they were reviewing or why the change order was never enforced.

commonly_wrong.claim: The tank failure was caused by a simple oversight in the wiring.
commonly_wrong.record: The switch was never classified 'flight-critical' because it only operated during ground procedures. NR issued a blanket requirement for 65V compatibility but did not explicitly list the internal thermostatic switch as needing a part change, and Beech continued installing the original 28V switches per the drawings on file.
commonly_wrong.source: Report of Apollo 13 Review Board, NASA TMX-65270, June 15, 1970
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The failure was not a single missed part. It was a requirement that was issued, never flowed down, and never checked at three separate points in the chain.

commonly_wrong.claim: Engineers saw the tank overheating during the March 1970 ground test.
commonly_wrong.record: The temperature gauge for the heater could only record up to 85 degrees F. Most of the individuals involved in the detanking discussion knew nothing of the extended heater and fan operation, so the off-nominal heating was invisible to them at the time.
commonly_wrong.source: Report of Apollo 13 Review Board, NASA TMX-65270, June 15, 1970
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The instrument that should have caught the fault physically could not read high enough to show it.

commonly_wrong.claim: The thermostat was upgraded to 65 volts along with the rest of the tank hardware.
commonly_wrong.record: The 1965 modification touched virtually every component except the thermostatic safety switches inside the oxygen tank heaters. Beech kept building tanks with the original 28V switch for four years.
commonly_wrong.source: Report of Apollo 13 Review Board, NASA TMX-65270, June 15, 1970
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: It is the one component the change order was actually about, and it is the one component the change never reached.

could_not_verify.item: Whether any pre-1970 safety recommendation specifically addressed the thermostat voltage rating gap before Apollo 13.
could_not_verify.note: No primary source located confirming or denying a prior recommendation on this specific gap.

could_not_verify.item: Which Cortright recommendation directly led to the thermostat upgrade and whether it was ever marked 'closed unacceptable' or revisited.
could_not_verify.note: Recommendation tracking status not confirmed in sources retrieved.

could_not_verify.item: Whether North American Rockwell documented the initial change order directing Beech to upgrade the thermostat, and if so, where it was archived.
could_not_verify.note: No archival record of the specific change order document was located.

location: Atlantic Ocean, off Cape Canaveral, Florida
agency: Rogers Commission (Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident)
the_unresolved_thing: NASA and Thiokol continued operating the field joint design and approving launches despite certification programs that neither agency understood to be adequate, and no post-Commission investigation ever settled what either agency believed it was actually reviewing when it certified the O-ring seal as flight-ready.

structural_test.why: The Rogers Commission concluded the O-ring flaw was known to NASA managers as early as 1977, and both NASA and Thiokol accepted the joint's unsuitability as a baseline rather than demanding redesign. The open question is not the failure sequence, it is why the certification process kept permitting flight of a component both agencies knew was eroding, and on what data.

commonly_wrong.claim: The night before the launch, Thiokol engineers warned NASA that the O-rings were dangerous, and NASA ignored them.
commonly_wrong.record: Thiokol management initially recommended against launching below 53 degrees. After NASA personnel challenged that reasoning and Thiokol requested a recess, Thiokol management reversed its own position and recommended proceeding with the launch.
commonly_wrong.source: Rogers Commission Report, Vol. 1, Ch. V-VI
commonly_wrong.why_it_matters: The warning did not go unheard. It was withdrawn by the same company that issued it, after NASA pushed back on the data, not the risk.

investigators_disagree.question: Did the Rogers Commission and the later Congressional investigation reach different conclusions on the immediate cause?
investigators_disagree.position_a: Rogers Commission: failure of the pressure seal in the aft field joint of the right solid rocket motor, due to a faulty design unacceptably sensitive to temperature, dynamic loading, and other factors.
investigators_disagree.position_b: House Committee on Science and Technology: affirms the same joint design flaw and finds neither NASA nor Thiokol fully understood the joint's operation prior to the accident.
investigators_disagree.status: No disagreement between the two bodies on the physical cause. The disagreement that never got resolved is upstream of both reports, in the certification and waiver process itself.

could_not_verify.item: The exact start time of the January 27 teleconference between Thiokol and NASA.
could_not_verify.note: Secondary sources cite 8:45 p.m. but this could not be confirmed against the primary Rogers Commission transcript.

could_not_verify.item: The statement attributed to NASA's Lawrence Mulloy: 'My God Thiokol, when do you want me to launch? Next April?'
could_not_verify.note: Appears only in secondary analysis, not in Rogers Commission testimony or hearing transcripts.

could_not_verify.item: The specific schedule pressure NASA managers cited to reverse Thiokol's no-launch position during the recess.
could_not_verify.note: The Commission describes generalized 'institutional pressure' but does not attribute a specific statement to a specific manager during the recess.

slides.headline: 73 seconds
slides.text: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff on January 28, 1986, killing all seven crew members.
slides.visual: Black frame, white type only. No launch photo on this slide.

slides.label: What everyone gets wrong
slides.headline: Thiokol didn't warn NASA. They reversed.
slides.text: The night before launch, Thiokol's engineers recommended against flying below 53 degrees. After NASA challenged the data and Thiokol took a recess, Thiokol management reversed that recommendation and cleared the launch.
slides.visual: Rogers Commission Report Vol. 1, Ch. V text excerpt, cropped tight.

slides.label: The safeguard that existed
slides.headline: 23 launches. Minimum temp: 53°F.
slides.text: Every prior shuttle flight had launched above 53 degrees Fahrenheit, the coldest data point Thiokol had for O-ring performance. Challenger launched at 36 degrees, 15 degrees below any flight on record.
slides.visual: Rogers Commission Report Vol. 1, Ch. VI temperature chart, document excerpt only.

slides.label: What NASA knew, and when
slides.headline: 1977: the joint rotation problem is already on paper.
slides.text: The Commission found NASA managers were aware of O-ring erosion and joint rotation concerns as early as 1977, nine years before the accident. Launches continued.
slides.visual: Rogers Commission Report Vol. 1, Ch. IV, document excerpt.

slides.label: Investigators disagree
slides.headline: Same joint. Same flaw. No agreement on why it was allowed.
slides.text: The Rogers Commission and the House Committee on Science and Technology both identified the same field joint design flaw. Neither report resolved how a joint with a documented erosion history kept receiving flight certification.
slides.visual: House Committee Report GPO-CRPT-99hrpt1016 cover page, document excerpt.

slides.label: The permission, not the mechanism
slides.headline: Waivers, not redesign.
slides.text: Rather than redesigning the joint after erosion was first observed, NASA and Thiokol treated each instance of O-ring erosion within a widening margin of what they considered 'acceptable risk,' a margin that expanded with each successful flight rather than contracting.
slides.visual: Rogers Commission Report Vol. 1, Ch. VI, 'acceptable risk' text excerpt.

slides.label: The recess
slides.headline: Thiokol asked for five minutes. Took thirty.
slides.text: During the January 27 teleconference, Thiokol engineers recommended against launch. NASA officials questioned the flight-readiness rationale. Thiokol requested a caucus, and returned roughly thirty minutes later with a reversed recommendation to launch.
slides.visual: Rogers Commission Report Vol. 1, Ch. V, teleconference summary excerpt.

slides.label: What the record shows
slides.headline: No new data. Same data, different conclusion.
slides.text: The Commission found that no new engineering data was introduced during the recess. The same temperature and erosion data was reinterpreted to support a different outcome.
slides.visual: Rogers Commission Report Vol. 1, Ch. VI, findings text excerpt.

slides.label: What was never settled
slides.headline: No investigation ever fixed what 'flight-ready' meant.
slides.text: Both NASA's certification process and Thiokol's engineering sign-off continued for years without a shared, documented standard for what data justified clearing a known erosion defect for flight. Neither the Rogers Commission nor Congress resolved what either organization believed it was actually reviewing when it certified the joint.
slides.visual: Rogers Commission Report Vol. 1, Ch. VI, closing findings page, document excerpt only.
